chapter.name: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science

questions.q: The page numbers of this book are framed by a magnifying glass and a compass. What does the compass remind us of?
o: That exploration needs direction: choosing models, asking the right questions and knowing the limits of our ideas
That science needs careful observation: noticing patterns that might otherwise be missed
That every scientific symbol comes from a Latin word
That science is divided into separate branches with fixed boundaries
questions.a: That exploration needs direction: choosing appropriate models, asking the right questions and knowing the limits of where our ideas apply.

questions.q: In a simple chemistry model, how are atoms and molecules usually drawn?
o: As a smooth sphere layered into regions
questions.a: As spheres and bonds (a single point is the physics model of a car, labelled diagrams are biology's cells, and the layered sphere is earth science's Earth).

questions.q: Sneha wants a simple model of how long her paper boat takes to float 10 m down a gentle stream. Which detail can she safely ignore?
o: The distance the boat must travel
The direction in which the water flows
questions.a: The colour of the paper: it makes no difference to the time taken, while the speed and direction of the water and the distance all matter.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the simple model of a cricket ball hit for a six, the mass of the ball is kept.
Reason (R): The mass of the ball makes no difference to whether the ball crosses the boundary without hitting the ground.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the chapter says the mass of the ball, and the speed and direction of the hit, are very important; it is the bat's brand, the ball's colour and the grass that make no difference.

questions.q: What is a scientific model? Give one example from the chapter of how a field of science uses a model.
questions.a: A model is a simplified way of looking at a real system that focuses only on what is most important for a given question. Example: in physics a moving car may be represented as a single point (or: cells shown as diagrams in biology, atoms as spheres and bonds in chemistry, the Earth as a layered sphere in earth science).
s: Model defined as a simplified way of looking at a real system that keeps what matters for the question
One correct example from the chapter (car as a point, atoms as spheres and bonds, cells as diagrams, or Earth as a layered sphere)

questions.q: In earth science, the Earth may be treated as a smooth sphere layered into distinct regions. (a) Name one real feature of the Earth's surface that this model leaves out. (b) Why is leaving it out not a mistake?
questions.a: (a) Mountains and valleys (the bumps and dips of the surface). (b) Details are left out on purpose to keep the model simple enough while still answering the question being studied, such as how the Earth is layered.
s: (a) a surface feature left out, such as mountains, valleys or the oceans' shape
(b) ignoring it is a deliberate choice that keeps the model simple and still answers the question

questions.q: State how each of these is shown in a simple model, as described in the chapter: (a) a moving car in physics, (b) cells in biology, (c) the Earth in earth science.
questions.a: (a) A moving car is represented as a single point. (b) Cells are shown as diagrams highlighting key parts. (c) The Earth is treated as a smooth sphere layered into distinct regions.
s: (a) a single point
(b) diagrams highlighting key parts
(c) a smooth sphere layered into distinct regions

questions.q: Two students model how long it takes to walk from the school gate to the library, 300 m away. Asha keeps the distance and her walking speed. Bunty keeps the colour of his shoes, the number of trees on the way and the name of the library, but not his speed. (a) Whose model can answer the question? (b) Give the reason. (c) Name one extra detail Asha could add later for greater accuracy.
questions.a: (a) Asha's model. (b) The time taken depends on the distance and the walking speed; shoe colour, trees and the library's name make no difference, and without his speed Bunty cannot find the time. (c) For example, the time spent waiting at a crossing or climbing stairs on the way; more complex models add extra details for greater accuracy.
s: (a) Asha's model
(b) distance and speed decide the time; Bunty's details make no difference and he lacks the speed
(c) a sensible extra detail that affects the time (waiting, stairs, slowing down)

questions.q:
A Class 9 team in Guwahati wants to know one thing: will a paper plane thrown from the first-floor corridor reach the far wall of the courtyard, 12 m away? They list everything they can think of: the colour of the plane, the speed of the throw (about 6 m/s), the direction of the throw, the mass of the plane (5 g), the brand of the paper, the name of the thrower, and a light breeze blowing across the courtyard.
(a) Name two listed details that make no difference and can be ignored.
(b) Ignoring the breeze for now, name the listed details their first simple model must keep.
(c) Is it a mistake to leave details out of the model? Give the chapter's view.
(d) The first model says the plane will reach 14 m, but it lands at 10 m. Should the team add the breeze to the model? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: the colour of the plane, the brand of the paper, the name of the thrower. (b) The speed of the throw, the direction of the throw and the mass of the plane. (c) No: details are ignored on purpose to keep the model simple enough while still answering the question. (d) Yes: the prediction is 4 m out, so a left-out effect matters here; as models are made more complex, extra details are added for greater accuracy, and the breeze (air) is the obvious one to add.
s: (a) two details that make no difference (colour, paper brand, thrower's name)
(b) speed, direction and mass of the plane kept
(c) leaving details out is deliberate, to keep the model simple yet useful
(d) yes, add the breeze, because the 4 m miss shows a left-out effect matters and more complex models add details for accuracy

questions.q:
A road-safety team models a car on a straight road as a single point moving at a steady 54 km/h (15 m/s).
(i) Using the model, find how many seconds the car takes to cover 300 m.
(ii) Explain why treating the car as a point is good enough for question (i).
(iii) Give one question about the same car that the point model cannot answer, and say why.
(iv) The compass on the book's page numbers stands for 'knowing the limits of where our ideas apply'. Using your answers to (ii) and (iii), judge whether the point model is a good model.
questions.a: (i) 300 / 15 = 20 s. (ii) The car's size and shape make no difference to how long it takes to cover 300 m, so only its speed and the distance matter. (iii) For example, 'Will the car fit into a 4 m parking space?' or 'Will its door hit a pillar?': a point has no length or width, so the model has left out exactly what the question needs. (iv) It is a good model for travel-time questions but not for size questions; a model is judged against the question it is built for, and knowing where it stops working is part of using it well.
s: (ii) size and shape do not affect the travel time, only speed and distance
(iii) a question that needs the car's size, with the reason that a point has no size
(iv) judgement: good for some questions, not others; a model has limits that must be known

questions.q: In science, which symbol is used for electric current?
questions.a: I (c is the speed of light, F is force and v is velocity).

questions.q:
Match each quantity in Column I with its symbol in Column II.
Column I: 1. Mass  2. Velocity  3. Force  4. Electric current
Column II: A. F  B. I  C. m  D. v
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: mass is m, velocity is v, force is F and electric current is I.

questions.q: State two reasons the chapter gives for basing measurements, such as the kilogram, on agreed international standards instead of local objects.
questions.a: Standard units allow scientific results to be compared, and they ensure fairness in daily life and trade (a kilogram of rice means the same amount everywhere).
s: Results can be compared
Fairness in daily life and trade

questions.q: True or False? Using standard (SI) units everywhere would have helped prevent the kind of error in the airplane fuel story. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The crew used a fuel density in pounds per litre instead of kilograms per litre; using standard (SI) units everywhere avoids such conversions and the errors they cause.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the error came from mixing pounds and kilograms; one standard unit avoids conversions and errors

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Scientific symbols are always the first letter of the English name of the quantity, like m for mass, v for velocity and F for force.' (a) Give the example from the chapter that shows he is wrong. (b) Where does that symbol come from? (c) Ravi decides to write the speed of light as 's' in his own notes because it is easier to remember. Using the chapter, explain why this would cause trouble when he shares his work.
questions.a: (a) The speed of light is denoted c, not s or l. (b) c comes from the Latin word celeritas, meaning speed. (c) Symbols are based on international agreements, so that scientists everywhere read them the same way; if he uses his own symbol, others may not understand his notes or may confuse s with another quantity, and his results cannot easily be compared. Science needs a shared language of symbols.
s: (a) the speed of light written as c
(b) from the Latin word celeritas, meaning speed
(c) symbols rest on international agreement; a private symbol breaks the shared language, so others cannot read or compare his work

questions.q: A school lab needs 2.5 kg of common salt for a class activity. The storeroom has one jar labelled '1,200 g' and another labelled '0.8 kg'. (a) How many grams of salt are in stock altogether? (b) How many more grams must be bought? (c) A helper adds 1,200 and 0.8 and reports '1,200.8 g in stock'. What went wrong, and which idea from the chapter would have prevented it?
questions.a: (a) 0.8 kg = 800 g, so 1,200 + 800 = 2,000 g. (b) 2.5 kg = 2,500 g, so 2,500 - 2,000 = 500 g more. (c) He added a value in grams to a value in kilograms as if they were the same unit; writing every amount in one standard unit avoids such conversions and errors, as the chapter says after the airplane fuel story.
s: (a) 2,000 g in stock
(b) 500 g more
(c) grams and kilograms mixed; one standard unit everywhere avoids the error

questions.q:
Nila in Kolkata and Joseph in Kochi do the same experiment and share their notes. Nila writes 'mass = 250 g, force = 2 N'. Joseph writes 'm = 0.25 kg, F = 2 N'.
(a) Which quantities do Joseph's symbols m and F stand for?
(b) Change Nila's mass into kilograms. Do the two notes give the same mass?
(c) Name the three things that, according to the chapter, make up the shared language of science.
(d) Why does science give everyday words such as force and work one specific meaning?
questions.a: (a) m is mass and F is force. (b) 250 g = 0.25 kg, so the two notes give the same mass. (c) Specific terms, symbols and units. (d) So that scientific ideas are communicated clearly and unambiguously, and scientists across the world can describe observations, compare results and build ideas together.
s: (a) m = mass, F = force
(b) 250 g = 0.25 kg, same mass
(c) terms, symbols and units
(d) clear, unambiguous communication so results can be compared worldwide

questions.q:
A student's lab note reads: 'm = 3, v = 4, F = 12, I = 2.'
(i) Name the quantity that each symbol stands for.
(ii) What is missing from every value, and why does that make the note hard for another lab to use?
(iii) A second student writes the mass as '3000' and says his note agrees with the first. Show how both could be correct, and what would have to be added to prove it.
(iv) Write one rule for lab notes that follows the chapter's idea of a shared language.
questions.a: (i) m is mass, v is velocity, F is force and I is electric current. (ii) The units are missing; every symbol must go with a defined unit, and without it another lab cannot compare results (3 could be grams or kilograms). (iii) 3 kg = 3,000 g, so both agree only if the first means kilograms and the second grams; the units kg and g must be written to show this. (iv) Write every value with its standard (SI) unit, so that scientists anywhere can compare results without confusion.
s: (i) mass, velocity, force, electric current
(ii) units missing, so results cannot be compared
(iii) 3 kg = 3,000 g; agreement shown only when the units kg and g are written
(iv) a rule to always write the standard unit with each value

questions.q: A bus moves at a steady 40 km/h. How far does it travel in 3 hours?
questions.a: 120 km, since distance = speed x time = 40 x 3.

questions.q: The chapter calls an equation 'a compact statement about how certain things are related'. For an object moving at a steady speed, distance = speed x time. What does this statement tell us?
o: At the same speed, doubling the time doubles the distance
Distance does not depend on time
At the same speed, doubling the time halves the distance
The speed changes whenever the time changes
questions.a: At the same speed, doubling the time doubles the distance: distance is speed multiplied by time, so it grows in step with time.

questions.q:
Read these statements about mathematics in science.
Statement I: Mathematics in science is meant to be a hurdle that only some students can cross.
Statement II: Learning to use mathematics in science mainly means memorising equations.
Statement III: Mathematical expressions are used to describe patterns of population growth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: III only: the chapter says mathematics is not meant to be a hurdle and that using it does not mean memorising equations, but it does describe population growth, reaction rates and energy changes.

questions.q: A biologist grows bacteria in a dish. She starts with 500 cells and finds that the number doubles every hour. Follow the chapter's order of thinking to find how many cells there are after 3 hours: (a) describe the situation, (b) name the quantities that matter, (c) use the relationship between them to find the number.
questions.a: (a) A population of bacteria that grows by doubling each hour (a pattern of population growth). (b) The starting number (500 cells), the time in hours and the doubling each hour. (c) After 1 h: 1,000; after 2 h: 2,000; after 3 h: 4,000 cells (500 x 2 x 2 x 2).
s: (a) situation: a population doubling every hour
(b) quantities: starting number, time, doubling per hour
(c) 4,000 cells after 3 hours

questions.q: In a chemistry lab, the gas given off by a reaction is measured every minute. The readings for the first four minutes are 10 mL, 20 mL, 30 mL and 40 mL. (a) Name the two quantities being related. (b) State in words how they are related.
questions.a: (a) The volume of gas given off and the time. (b) The volume of gas rises by 10 mL every minute, so it grows steadily with time (the reaction gives off gas at a steady rate).
s: (a) volume of gas and time
(b) volume rises by 10 mL each minute, steadily with time

questions.q: True or False? According to the chapter, an equation in science is just a tool for getting numerical answers. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. An equation is not just a calculation tool; it is a compact statement about how certain things are related, and mathematics is a language for thinking, not just for finding numbers.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: an equation is a compact statement of how quantities are related, a language for thinking

questions.q:
Ira and Om leave the same gate at 7:00 am for a school 6 km away along one road. Ira walks at a steady 5 km/h and Om cycles at a steady 15 km/h.
(a) At what time does Ira reach school?
(b) At what time does Om reach school?
(c) How far is Ira from the school when Om arrives?
(d) School assembly starts at 7:45 am. Ira says she will still leave at 7:00 am and just walk faster. Find the steady speed she would need, decide whether that is sensible for walking, and say what she should do instead.
questions.a: (a) 6 / 5 = 1.2 h = 72 min, so 8:12 am. (b) 6 / 15 = 0.4 h = 24 min, so 7:24 am. (c) In 0.4 h Ira walks 5 x 0.4 = 2 km, so she is 6 - 2 = 4 km from school. (d) She has 45 min = 0.75 h, so she needs 6 / 0.75 = 8 km/h, which is a jog rather than a walk and hard to keep up for 6 km. At her usual 5 km/h she needs 72 min, so she should leave by 6:33 am (or cycle with Om).
s: (a) 72 min, 8:12 am
(b) 24 min, 7:24 am
(c) Ira has walked 2 km, so 4 km from school
(d) needs 8 km/h, not sensible for walking; leave by 6:33 am or cycle

questions.q:
Meena's phone starts fully charged (100%). While she watches videos, its charge drops steadily by 8% every hour.
(i) What is the charge after 1 hour?
(ii) What is the charge after 5 hours?
(iii) After how many hours does the charge fall to 20%?
(iv) Write in words the relationship between the charge left and the time.
(v) Apart from motion, name the three kinds of change the chapter says mathematical expressions are used to describe.
questions.a: (i) 100 - 8 = 92%. (ii) 100 - 5 x 8 = 60%. (iii) It must fall by 80%, and 80 / 8 = 10 hours. (iv) Charge left = 100% minus 8% for every hour of watching. (v) Rates of chemical reactions, patterns of population growth and changes in energy within a system.
s: (iii) 10 hours
(iv) charge left = 100% minus 8% per hour, in words
(v) reaction rates, population growth, energy changes

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does a law in science usually do?
o: Describes a regular pattern observed in nature
Explains why a pattern occurs, using evidence gathered over time
Gives a broad idea that helps us make sense of a given situation
States a guess that has not yet been tested
questions.a: Describes a regular pattern observed in nature, often in words or mathematical relationships (explaining why is the work of a theory; a broad idea is a principle).

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as its example of a principle?
o: Conservation of energy applied when climbing up the stairs
Newton's laws of motion explaining the jerk when a bus stops suddenly
The atomic theory explaining how molecules are formed
Treating the matter in a star as a hot gas
questions.a: Conservation of energy applied when climbing up the stairs (the bus jerk is the example of a law, molecules of a theory, and the hot-gas star is a model).

questions.q:
Match each example in Column I with the term the chapter uses for it in Column II.
Column I: 1. The pattern of the jerk felt when a bus stops suddenly  2. Explaining how molecules are formed  3. Applying an idea about energy when climbing up the stairs  4. Treating a star's matter as a hot gas to explain its colour
Column II: A. A model  B. A law  C. A principle  D. A theory
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-C, 4-A: Newton's laws of motion for the bus, the atomic theory for molecules, the principle of conservation of energy for the stairs, and Saha's hot-gas model of a star.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In science, a theory does not mean a guess.
Reason (R): A scientific theory is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a theory is not a guess precisely because it rests on careful testing and critical examination.

questions.q: Rina says, 'The atomic theory has been tested so carefully that it can never change.' Correct her using two points from the chapter.
questions.a: Scientific ideas, theories included, are always open to improvement and often change as new evidence becomes available; and a theory is based on the evidence available at that time, so no scientific theory is ever final or beyond question.
s: Theories stay open to improvement and change with new evidence
A theory rests on evidence available at that time; no theory is final or beyond question

questions.q: True or False? A principle is an explanation of why a pattern in nature occurs, based on evidence gathered over time. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. That describes a theory. A principle is a broad idea that helps us make sense of a given situation, such as conservation of energy applied when climbing up the stairs.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: that is a theory; a principle is a broad idea that helps make sense of a given situation

questions.q: The chapter says a theory is usually based on 'evidence gathered over time and available at that time'. (a) What do the words 'available at that time' tell us about a theory? (b) What happens to a theory when new evidence becomes available? (c) Why does the chapter call this a feature that makes science reliable, not unreliable?
questions.a: (a) A theory explains what the evidence known so far shows; later evidence may not have been available when it was made. (b) It may be improved or changed. (c) Because science follows the evidence and corrects itself, its ideas get better over time instead of staying fixed by opinion.
s: (a) a theory rests on the evidence known so far, and more may come
(b) it is improved or changed
(c) correcting itself by evidence makes science reliable

questions.q: A school magazine prints this line: 'Newton's laws of motion are just a theory, and a theory is only a guess, so we should not rely on them.' Evaluate the line in steps. (a) Using the chapter's terms, is it correct to call Newton's laws of motion a theory? (b) Is a theory only a guess? (c) Does the fact that scientific ideas can be improved mean we should not rely on them? (d) Rewrite the line so that it agrees with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) No: the chapter uses Newton's laws as its example of laws, which describe regular patterns (such as the jerk when a bus stops suddenly); a theory explains why patterns occur. (b) No: a theory is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination. (c) No: openness to improvement as new evidence arrives is a key feature that makes science reliable. (d) For example: 'Newton's laws of motion describe regular patterns in motion; like all scientific ideas they are open to improvement, which is why science can be relied on.'
s: (a) Newton's laws are laws (patterns), not a theory
(b) a theory is a tested explanation, not a guess
(c) openness to improvement makes science reliable
(d) a corrected line consistent with the chapter

questions.q:
(i) In one line each, say what a law, a theory and a principle does in science, as the chapter describes them.
(ii) Give the chapter's example of a law and of a theory.
(iii) Classify each statement as a law or a theory, and justify: X: 'A ball thrown straight up always comes back down.' Y: 'Matter is made of tiny particles, and evidence about these particles explains why sugar seems to disappear when it dissolves in water.'
(iv) A friend says a theory becomes final once it is proved. Using the chapter, say why this is wrong.
questions.a: (i) A law describes a regular pattern observed in nature; a theory explains why such patterns occur, based on evidence; a principle is a broad idea that helps us make sense of a given situation. (ii) Law: Newton's laws of motion (the jerk when a bus stops suddenly); theory: the atomic theory (how molecules are formed). (iii) X is a law: it only describes a pattern seen again and again, without saying why. Y is a theory: it gives an explanation of why something happens, built on evidence. (iv) No scientific theory is ever final; even successful theories have limits and may fail under new conditions or more precise measurement, and they change as new evidence becomes available.
s: (i) law describes, theory explains why, principle is a broad idea for a situation
(ii) Newton's laws (bus); atomic theory (molecules)
(iii) X is a law, because it describes a pattern
(iii) Y is a theory, because it explains why, based on evidence
(iv) no theory is final; theories have limits and change with new evidence

questions.q: How does the chapter describe a scientific prediction?
o: A reasoned expectation based on evidence and careful thinking
A lucky guess that sometimes turns out right
A fixed fact that can never fail
An opinion that most people agree with
questions.a: A reasoned expectation based on evidence and careful thinking, not a guess.

questions.q: Which prediction does the chapter say can be made using biological principles?
o: How one's breathing would change while running
How far a kicked football will travel
How much carbon dioxide a reaction will produce
How soft a baked bread would be
questions.a: How one's breathing would change while running (the football uses ideas about motion; carbon dioxide and bread use knowledge of chemical reactions).

questions.q:
Read these statements about prediction in science.
Statement I: Well-established laws, theories and models let us anticipate what will happen even in cases where we cannot perform an experiment.
Statement II: Weather forecasts are usually reliable for a few hours or even a few days.
Statement III: To test a prediction, questions with simple yes/no answers are usually the most useful.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only: the chapter says good questions look for measurable evidence and past patterns, and that yes/no questions are usually not so useful.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A weather forecast for the next two hours is usually more reliable than one for two weeks ahead.
Reason (R): Weather forecasts use measurements and models.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: all forecasts use measurements and models, so that cannot explain why short forecasts are better; the reason is that very tiny differences in conditions grow over time, making forecasts less certain further ahead.

questions.q: Raju says, 'It will be very hot tomorrow because I can feel it.' (a) Is this prediction based on measurable evidence? (b) Write one question that would make it scientifically testable.
questions.a: (a) No, it rests on a feeling, not on measurable evidence or past patterns. (b) For example: 'What was the temperature today and on the last few days, and is it rising?' or 'What did the temperature do the last time the sky and wind were like this?'
s: (a) No, it is based on a feeling
(b) a question that asks for measurable data or a past pattern

questions.q: True or False? Science can make predictions about some situations even when an experiment on them cannot be performed. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. When laws, theories and models are well established, they let us anticipate what will happen under new conditions, before an experiment and in many cases even if we cannot perform one.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: well-established laws, theories and models let us anticipate outcomes without the experiment

questions.q: The chapter gives examples of predictions from three areas. Give one example of what can be predicted using (a) ideas about motion, (b) knowledge of chemical reactions, (c) biological principles.
questions.a: (a) How far a kicked football will travel. (b) How much carbon dioxide will be produced, or how soft a baked bread would be. (c) How one's breathing would change while running.
s: (a) how far a kicked football travels
(b) carbon dioxide produced or softness of baked bread
(c) change in breathing while running

questions.q:
A farmer near Nashik checked one weather app for 30 days, comparing each forecast with the weather that actually came. Forecasts made 1 day ahead were right on 27 of the 30 days, forecasts made 5 days ahead on 21 days, and forecasts made 10 days ahead on 15 days.
(a) Find the percentage of correct forecasts for each.
(b) Describe the pattern in your answers.
(c) Give the chapter's reason for this pattern.
(d) The farmer must decide when to spray his crop, which needs a dry day. Should he plan by the 10-day forecast or wait for the 1-day forecast? Justify with your answers.
questions.a: (a) 1 day: 27/30 = 90%; 5 days: 21/30 = 70%; 10 days: 15/30 = 50%. (b) The further ahead the forecast, the less often it is right. (c) Weather depends on many changing factors (temperature, pressure, humidity, wind), and very tiny differences in conditions grow over time. (d) He can use the 10-day forecast only as a rough plan, since it is right only half the time, and should confirm with the 1-day forecast (90%) before spraying.
s: (b) accuracy falls as the forecast looks further ahead
(c) many changing factors; tiny differences grow over time
(d) a decision using the percentages: confirm with the 1-day forecast

questions.q:
A science club lets a ball roll down a ramp from three different heights and uses a simple model of motion to predict how far it rolls along the floor. Predicted: 25 m, 30 m and 35 m. Measured: 24 m, 29 m and 28 m.
(i) Find the difference between predicted and measured distance for each roll.
(ii) Which predictions match the observations well, and which does not?
(iii) According to the chapter, what should the club do when a prediction does not match?
(iv) Suggest one assumption in their simple model that they should check, with a reason.
(v) A member says, 'One bad prediction proves our science is useless.' Evaluate this.
questions.a: (i) 1 m, 1 m and 7 m. (ii) The first two match well (1 m out); the third does not (7 m out). (iii) Re-examine their assumptions, model or measurements. (iv) For example, that the friction of the floor (or air resistance) can be ignored: the fastest roll, from the greatest height, may be slowed more by it, so the left-out detail may matter. (v) Wrong: when predictions match, confidence grows; when they do not, scientists re-examine and improve the model, so a failed prediction drives deeper understanding and is a strength of science.
s: (ii) first two match, the third does not
(iii) re-examine assumptions, model or measurements
(iv) a sensible assumption to check, with reason
(v) a mismatch leads to improvement, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: According to the chapter, about how many kilocalories does an average adult need per day?
questions.a: 2000 to 2500 kcal per day.

questions.q: To estimate breaths in a day, you need the number of minutes in a day. What is it?
questions.a: 1440, since 60 x 24 = 1440 minutes (3600 is seconds in an hour; 86,400 is seconds in a day).

questions.q: Om takes 15 breaths a minute at rest, and each breath is about 0.5 litre. About how much air does he breathe in one hour?
questions.a: 450 litres: 15 x 0.5 = 7.5 litres a minute, and 7.5 x 60 = 450 litres an hour.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An estimate of a few tonnes of rice a month for a family of four is far too much.
Reason (R): Science values careful reasoning perhaps much more than accurate calculations.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the estimate is too much because a family of four could not eat that much rice in a month; R is a general statement about what science values.

questions.q: Kiran finds that 6 breaths fill a 3-litre beach ball. (a) About how much air is in one of her breaths? (b) If she takes 14 breaths a minute, about how many litres does she breathe in a minute?
questions.a: (a) 3 / 6 = 0.5 litre. (b) 14 x 0.5 = 7 litres a minute.
s: (a) 0.5 litre
(b) 7 litres a minute

questions.q: In the balloon cross-check, Leela takes 30 s, not 20 s, to blow up each 2-litre balloon. (a) How many litres would she blow in a minute? (b) Using 1440 minutes in a day, how many litres would that give per day?
questions.a: (a) 2 balloons a minute x 2 litres = 4 litres a minute. (b) 4 x 1440 = 5,760 litres a day.
s: (a) 4 litres a minute
(b) 5,760 litres a day

questions.q: Make a rough estimate of rice for a family of four, assuming all their calories come from rice. Take 2000 kcal per person per day and, as a round figure, 400 kcal from 100 g of uncooked rice. (a) How many kcal does the family need per day? (b) How many grams of rice is that per day? (c) About how many kilograms in a 30-day month?
s: (a) 8,000 kcal
(b) 2,000 g a day
(c) about 60 kg a month

questions.q: Tara counts 12 breaths a minute at rest and estimates that she breathes in only 500 litres of air in a whole day. (a) Using 1440 minutes in a day, how many breaths does she take in a day? (b) What volume of air per breath does her 500-litre total imply? (c) The chapter's balloon method gives about 0.5 litre per breath. Which of her figures must be wrong, and about how many times too small is it?
questions.a: (a) 12 x 1440 = 17,280 breaths. (b) 500 / 17,280 = about 0.03 litre (about 29 mL) per breath. (c) Her breath count was measured, so the 500-litre total must be wrong: it implies about 0.03 litre a breath, so about 70 breaths would be needed to fill a 2-litre balloon instead of 4-5. With 0.5 litre per breath the day's total is about 8,640 litres, so her figure is about 17 times too small.
s: (a) 17,280 breaths a day
(b) about 0.03 litre per breath
(c) the 500-litre total is wrong, about 17 times too small

questions.q:
A school in Pune is taking 40 students on a 3-day nature camp and must carry drinking water. A teacher estimates that each student drinks about 2.5 litres a day. Water comes in 20-litre cans, and the bus has room for only 18 cans.
(a) Estimate the litres needed for all students for one day.
(b) Estimate the litres needed for the whole camp, and the number of cans.
(c) On a hot day each student may drink about 3.5 litres. How many litres would three hot days need, and how many cans is that?
(d) Decide whether the 18 cans the bus can carry are enough, and what the school should plan. Justify with your numbers.
questions.a: (a) 40 x 2.5 = 100 litres. (b) 100 x 3 = 300 litres, which is 300 / 20 = 15 cans. (c) 40 x 3.5 x 3 = 420 litres, which is 21 cans. (d) 18 cans hold 360 litres: enough for the normal estimate (300 litres) and even for one hot day (100 + 100 + 140 = 340 litres), but not for three hot days (420 litres). So the school should take all 18 cans and arrange a refill at the camp in case the weather stays hot.
s: (a) 100 litres a day
(b) 300 litres, 15 cans
(c) 420 litres, 21 cans
(d) 18 cans = 360 litres: enough for normal days and one hot day, not three; take 18 and plan a refill

questions.q: Besides its own branches, which areas does the chapter say science connects with naturally?
o: Mathematics, technology, arts and social sciences
questions.a: Mathematics, technology, arts and social sciences, each enriching the other.

questions.q: A team is designing a cheaper water purifier, run by sunlight, for a village. Which statement fits the chapter?
o: The project needs ideas from several disciplines together
It needs only earth science, because it is about a village's water supply
It is a technology problem, so science is not needed for it
It needs only physics, because the purifier runs on sunlight
questions.a: The project needs ideas from several disciplines together: designing sustainable technologies is one of the chapter's examples of real-world problems that cross the branches, and science connects naturally with technology rather than being replaced by it.

questions.q: The chapter says science is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration and what else?
questions.a: Careful questioning.

questions.q:
Match each branch in Column I with what it contributes to understanding how a mask works (Column II).
Column I: 1. Physics  2. Chemistry  3. Biology  4. Mathematics
Column II: A. Properties of polymer fibres  B. Modelling airflow and filtration efficiency  C. Size and behaviour of viruses  D. Particle motion and electrostatic attraction
questions.a: 1-D, 2-A, 3-C, 4-B: physics gives particle motion and electrostatic attraction, chemistry the polymer fibres, biology the viruses, and mathematics the airflow and filtration model.

questions.q:
Read these statements about science as a human activity.
Statement I: Developing medicines requires ideas from several disciplines together.
Statement II: Science has grown mainly through the work of a single culture in one generation.
Statement III: Scientific thinking helps a person evaluate information critically.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only: the chapter says science develops through many individuals across different cultures and generations.

questions.q: State two ways in which, according to the chapter, scientific thinking helps you even if you do not study science after Grade 10.
questions.a: It helps you understand the technology that surrounds you, and it helps you evaluate information critically and make sense of the world you live in.
s: Understanding the technology around you
Evaluating information critically and making sense of the world

questions.q: (a) Why does the chapter say that physics, chemistry, biology and earth science are not real boundaries in nature? (b) Using climate change, say what this means for solving real-world problems.
questions.a: (a) The divisions are made by us only to help organise knowledge; the natural world has no such boundaries and the branches are not independent of each other. (b) A problem such as understanding climate change needs ideas from several disciplines together, not from one branch alone.
s: (a) branches are human divisions to organise knowledge, not boundaries in nature
(b) climate change needs several disciplines together

questions.q:
A town in Rajasthan plans a rainwater-harvesting project for its schools. The project has four tasks: T1 - calculate how big each tank must be from the roof's area and a given yearly rainfall figure; T2 - choose a tank material that will not react with the water; T3 - check that the stored water has no harmful germs; T4 - study how rain soaks into the soil and refills the ground below. The budget pays for only three experts, chosen from a mathematician, a chemist, a biologist and an earth scientist.
(a) Which expert suits each task?
(b) The chemist says, 'I can choose the tank material, so I alone can make sure the water is safe to drink.' Why is this not enough?
(c) What does this project show about the branches of science?
(d) Decide which three experts to hire and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) T1 mathematician (a calculation from given figures), T2 chemist, T3 biologist, T4 earth scientist. (b) Safe water needs both a tank that does not react with the water (chemistry) and water free of harmful germs, which are living things studied in biology; so the chemist needs the biologist as well. (c) A real-world problem needs ideas from several disciplines together; the branches are divisions we make, not boundaries in nature. (d) Any choice justified by the tasks: for example, hire the mathematician, chemist and biologist because tank size, safe material and germ-free water decide whether the system works at all, and leave the soil question for later; or keep the earth scientist if refilling the ground is the main aim.
s: (a) T1 mathematician, T2 chemist, T3 biologist, T4 earth scientist
(b) safe water also needs germ checks, which is biology, so the chemist alone is not enough
(c) real problems need several disciplines; branches are human divisions
(d) a choice of three justified by the tasks and the project's aim
